title: India Targets $44 Billion Space Economy as Private Sector Fuels Five-Fold Growth
excerpt: The country aims to capture 8-10% of the global space market within a decade, backed by 400-plus startups, surging commercial revenues and new satellite broadband ambitions.
body:
• India aims to grow its space economy five-fold from $8.5 billion to $44 billion over the next decade, targeting 8-10% of the global market.
  • The country now has more than 400 space startups, up from just one in 2014, with cumulative investment crossing $500 million.
  • Private companies including Skyroot Aerospace have achieved milestones such as independent rocket launches, while Jio has announced plans for 1,600 LEO broadband satellites.
  • NewSpace India Limited revenues surged from Rs 321 crore in FY22 to Rs 3,246 crore in FY25, reflecting rapid commercialisation of ISRO-developed technologies.

India's space sector is undergoing its most significant transformation since the country's first satellite launch five decades ago, with private industry driving an ambitious push to capture a much larger share of the global space economy.

Lt. Gen. AK Bhatt, Director General of the Indian Space Association (ISpA), said in an interview with ANI this week that India currently accounts for about 2-2.5% of the roughly $400 billion global space economy — around $8.5 billion. The country aims to grow that share to 8-10% within the next decade, putting the target at approximately $44 billion.

"The private sector is now participating to provide services in all domains, be it communication, be it ISR, and in future, maybe PNT to all users, military and so on."

— Lt. Gen. AK Bhatt, Director General, Indian Space Association

Private Players Reshape the Landscape

The numbers tell a striking story of transformation. From a single registered space startup in 2014, India now has more than 400, according to a government fact-sheet released in June. Investment in Indian space startups has crossed $500 million, with nearly $150 million attracted in 2025 alone.

https://x.com/Sputnik_India/status/2096489827159925095

Skyroot Aerospace has emerged as the most prominent private player, becoming the first Indian company to successfully launch a rocket. Five to six other companies have now launched their own satellites, according to Bhatt. The armed forces have awarded contracts for satellite-based surveillance services, and a separate contract for 12 Earth observation satellites has gone to private firms.

On the commercial side, NewSpace India Limited (NSIL) — the agency created to commercialise ISRO-developed technologies — has seen revenues surge from Rs 321.77 crore in FY22 to Rs 3,246.09 crore in FY25, a roughly ten-fold increase in three years.

Where the $44 Billion Will Come From

A FICCI-EY report presented at the Bharat Space Conclave projects satellite communication (SATCOM) as the largest revenue segment at $14.8 billion by 2033, followed by navigation at over $9 billion and Earth observation at $8 billion. Exports could contribute $11 billion of the total, with upstream activities like launch services and satellite manufacturing accounting for about $32 billion.

But Bhatt emphasised that applications — not hardware — will be the biggest driver. Agriculture, disaster management, education and medical services are areas where space technology can be deployed domestically and exported globally.

"In those 44 billion, it will be money earned from launch vehicles, money earned from satellites. But most importantly, the economy is applications."

— Lt. Gen. AK Bhatt, Director General, Indian Space Association

Satellite Broadband Race Heats Up

Low-Earth orbit satellite broadband is emerging as a major battleground. Bhatt noted that SpaceX's Starlink operates about 10,000 satellites, Eutelsat OneWeb has around 640 and Amazon's Project Kuiper has launched approximately 396. Indian conglomerate Jio has announced plans for around 1,600 LEO satellites for broadband services.

Cost, however, remains the central challenge. Satellite broadband is still more expensive than terrestrial alternatives, and bridging that gap will be critical for rural and remote connectivity — areas where fibre is difficult or expensive to deploy.

Policy Gaps Remain

The government has taken several steps to liberalise the sector, including the Indian Space Policy 2023, liberalised foreign direct investment norms, a Rs 1,000 crore venture capital fund and a Rs 500 crore technology adoption fund. ISRO's spectrum for space communication will be allocated administratively rather than through auction, with the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India recommending charges at 4% of adjusted gross revenue.

But a dedicated Space Act — legislation that would define the regulator and address liability issues — has yet to materialise. Industry leaders say this is the single biggest remaining policy gap.

Global Ambitions

India has launched 399 foreign satellites since 2014 and signed more than 300 space cooperation agreements with 61 countries and five multilateral organisations. Active partnerships with NASA, JAXA, the European Space Agency and the French space agency CNES continue to expand.

The NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar (NISAR) satellite is already providing data globally, while India and Japan are collaborating on future lunar exploration. ISRO's own mission pipeline includes the Gaganyaan human spaceflight programme, the Bharatiya Antariksh Station, the Venus Orbiter Mission and the recent successful launch of GSLV-F17 carrying EOS-05, India's first geosynchronous imaging satellite.

For the Indian diaspora, the space boom offers both investment opportunities and a growing pool of high-skilled jobs in a sector that barely existed a decade ago. With the $44 billion target now official policy, the question is no longer whether India's space sector will grow — but whether private industry can deliver at the scale the government envisions.
